gaps.text: Combining several spectroscopy methods (data fusion) (Both channels look at the same spot through one probe head, so the two blocks can be fused at low level after block scaling, with one model per method kept as the baseline. Acquisition rates differ between the two methods, so the blocks must be aligned to a common time step and each instrument keeps its own calibration and diagnostics. The fused model must beat the best single method on held-out samples, otherwise the extra channel is dropped.)

items.finding: The source describes low-level data fusion as the simplest way to combine inputs by rearranging variables from different sources into one new data matrix.
items.how_it_applies: This supports the proposed low-level fusion of the two blocks after block scaling, but the source does not address differing acquisition rates or time-step alignment.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: It is a general PAT review, not a study of MIR ATR and fluorescence on the same probe head or of model biological tissues, so transfer to this interface and sample set is uncertain.

citation.quote: Low-level data fusion (LLDF) is considered the simplest method to achieve a combination of inputs. In this case, the data is rearranged into a new data matrix, where the variables coming from different sources are placed one after the other.

dropped.finding: The source reports that FTIR and fluorescence spectroscopy have been used together for edible oil authenticity, and that combining the two techniques improved robustness of the detection system.
dropped.how_it_applies: This could support testing a fused MIR ATR plus fluorescence model against the best single method, as the gap requires, but it does not establish that fusion will beat the single method for the laboratory classification study.
dropped.limits_and_transfer_risks: The work concerns edible oil authenticity, not model biological tissues, and the quoted comparison does not describe a single probe head, common time step, or the same instrument calibration.
